blocks.text: In making medicines, chirality is critical for safety and effectiveness. Living systems are built from chiral building blocks, and drug receptors act as highly specific chiral locks, so the two enantiomers of a chiral drug often have very different effects.

blocks.alt: Thalidomide: a benzene ring (drawn with a circle) fused to a five-membered ring with two C=O groups and an N. The N is joined by a dashed bond to a carbon of a six-membered ring that also has two C=O groups and an N-H; that carbon carries an H on a solid wedge.
blocks.caption: Figure 19.7: Thalidomide (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 19.7).

blocks.text: Thalidomide was first sold as a racemic mixture and seemed a very successful, non-toxic sedative (tranquilliser) with no known side effects. In the early 1960s, however, it was found that women given it for nausea ('morning sickness') in early pregnancy had babies with severe deformities, and the drug was withdrawn at once. Research showed that the (+) isomer was an effective and safe tranquilliser while the (-) isomer harmed the fetus. At first the problem was blamed on contamination by the (-) isomer in some batches, but later work showed that the pure (+) isomer racemises rapidly in the bloodstream: within 10 minutes the racemisation is more than 50% complete. Thalidomide will never be marketed again, although analogues, that are chirality stable are being, investigated as possible anti-inflammatory drugs.

blocks.text: Thalidomide has since been marketed again under strict controls: it was approved in the USA in 1998 for a complication of leprosy and in 2006 for multiple myeloma, with a pregnancy-prevention programme.
